study.title: Psalm 129 Old distress, faithful preservation, and judgment upon the enemies of Zion
study.overview: This song of the steps recalls the long history of suffering of the people of God, but does so to affirm two central truths: the Lord kept Israel standing despite repeated persecutions, and opposition against Zion will not have the final word. The psalm alternates memory, confession of God's righteousness and imprection against those who hate Zion. It ends with the image of a frustrated harvest, suggesting fruitless defeat for enemies and absence of blessing on his work.

outline.title: Israel recalls distress from youth
outline.explanation: The psalmist speaks in the name of Israel as of someone who suffered many times since his youth, but whose suffering he has not managed to destroy him. Language points to a prolonged history of oppression, presented as a public testimony of divine preservation.

outline.title: The pain was deep, but the Lord was just
outline.explanation: The image of the farmers who groove their backs describes severe and humiliating aggression. Against this violence, the text affirms the righteousness of the Lord, who broke the cords of the wicked, that is, interrupted his dominion and delivered his people.

outline.title: Prayer against the enemies of Zion and metaphor of the frustrated harvest
outline.explanation: The psalm asks for shame and setback for those who hate Zion. Then he compares such enemies to the roof grass, dry and profitless, and to a harvest so poor that neither the reaper gives himself to the work of collecting. The closure even denies the greeting of blessing, indicating sterility and disapproval.

study.context: The notes describe this psalm as a step of steps linked to Israel's public concerns. The reading of several commentators understands that the people look back, to the ancient tribulations, especially slavery in Egypt, and also for later deliverances. There is also the possibility, mentioned in the notes, of composition in the period of Babylonian exile or at the time of return; however, this appears as a hypothesis, not as textual certainty.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the history of God's people can be marked by repeated distress without this means final defeat. Divine fidelity appears in the preservation of the people over time and in the interruption of the plans of the wicked. There is here a moral vision of the world: God is just, he watches for Zion, and judges those who hate his cause, his ways and his people. At the same time, the image of the frustrated harvest communicates that evil can even hurt deeply, but does not produce lasting fruit when it opposes the Lord. In the evangelical confessional key, many see in this psalm a pattern applicable to God's people at any time: the church faces real opposition, but remains sustained by the faithful action of the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm summarizes the history of Israel into two parts: ancient distress and redemption, culminating in the image of the small or ignored harvest, which shows how enemies produce little result against the people of God.
The psalm can be sung as prayer and hope of the church of God in all ages, which has endured many storms and still faces enemies.
The salutation of the reapers is taken as an image of a non-existent or sterile harvest; thus, the text suggests that the land of the enemies will be desolate and without fruit.

questions: What memories of deliverance help God's people to interpret prolonged sufferings without despair?
How does the claim that the Lord is just correct our reading of the oppression suffered by the faithful?
What does it mean, in practice, to desire that the plans contrary to God end in shame and failure, without turning it into personal revenge?
study.practice: This psalm can be used in community prayer to remember past sufferings and recognize God's faithfulness over time. It also calls us not to measure the presence of the Lord only by immediate pressure, but by his ability to preserve his church despite repeated attacks. In practice, it is worth remembering concrete deliveries, thank you for the righteousness of God and ask that all opposition to its purpose lose strength and fruit. At the same time, the text teaches us to trust that the Lord knows how to interrupt the power of the wicked without abandoning his people.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow for sure to fix the exact date, author or historical occasion of the psalm. It is also not possible to state safely, from only these notes, whether references to Egypt, Babylon or harvesting should be read in a strictly literal, historical or just as poetic and collective language.
